title: What Makes the Difference to Student Progress?
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Dominic Salles uses a business thought experiment about YouTube thumbnails to introduce a 10X mindset: ask how to multiply the return on effort instead of chasing marginal gains. He then applies it to a Do Now in which students answer five recall questions in ten minutes and typically complete three. Coaching the teacher to circulate and narrate gets perhaps a 2X gain, but converting the Do Now into a self-marking quiz with twenty questions yields far more. He compounds the effect with spaced repetition across the year, sharing among five teachers, and the homework and marking time saved. The argument is deliberately provocative and arithmetic rather than empirical, and it ends by claiming a refusal to do this sacrifices pupil progress. The page ends with promotional services copy.
points: Changing the curriculum task, here a longer self-marking quiz, changes teacher behavior more reliably than coaching a hard-to-change habit.
Spacing the same retrieval Do Now at expanding gaps across the year multiplies its benefit well beyond a single use.
Sharing quizzes across a department multiplies impact and also reduces workload through reuse and automatic marking.
The business analogy frames improvement as multiplying return on effort rather than adding small increments.
The compounding numbers are illustrative and conservative adjustments are admitted, so the argument works as a heuristic, not evidence.
quotes: So, business is about taking a skill or a product and trying to maximise its impact on profit. Schools are about teaching students and trying to maximise the impact on progress. The thought process, the mindset, the way of looking, is the same in both.

I notice that most of the class only answer 3 out of 5 questions in this time limit. My feedback could be to circulate as soon as the register is done, and track the students as soon as they begin. Narrate what you are seeing - for example walk each row, calling out the number completed by each child, “3, 1, 2, 0, 3” and so on.

If the students have devices, they can do the form online. They will all finish 20 questions. All the questions will be automatically marked, with your teaching notes to get rid of misconceptions - you’ve already typed those in advance.
We have to space them in doubled gaps - 1 day, 3 days, 1 week, 2 weeks, 1 month, 2 months, 4 months. That’s 8 months in total.

Your teaching will be 10X more effective if you make Google quizzes for your Do Now. If you choose not to do that, and settle for a 5 question Do Now, you are deliberately sacrificing the progress of your students to your own desires.

If you don’t plan for the spacing of these retrievals across the year for the whole team, then your department are 50X less effective than they could be. You are sacrificing the the results of the whole cohort because you want to preserve your freedom to spend more time working harder but doing less.
